title: He Delighteth in Mercy
sections: “What doth the Lord require of thee?”
The Lord is both powerful and merciful
I can trust the Lord’s will and His timing
“Seek ye the Lord, all ye meek of the earth.”
The Lord will rejoice with His people in Zion

sayings.text: O my people, what have I done unto thee? and wherein have I wearied thee?
sayings.speaker: The Lord, to His people
sayings.why: In Micah 6 the Lord brings a case against His people, like a trial. He asks them to name one way He has let them down. He had only blessed them.

sayings.text: But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD
sayings.speaker: Micah, about himself
sayings.why: Other prophets in Micah’s day said whatever they were paid to say (Micah 3:11). Micah had the Spirit, so he told the people the truth about their sins.

sayings.text: But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah
sayings.speaker: Micah, about the Messiah
sayings.why: About 700 years before Jesus was born, Micah named His birthplace. When the Wise Men came, Herod’s advisers found the answer in this verse (Matthew 2:5–6).

sayings.text: he retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy
sayings.speaker: Micah, about the Lord
sayings.why: Micah ends his book asking, “Who is a God like unto thee?” The Lord doesn’t hold on to His anger. He loves to forgive.

sayings.text: The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble
sayings.speaker: Nahum, about the Lord
sayings.why: Nahum’s book announces the fall of cruel Nineveh. But in chapter 1 he stops to say that the Lord shelters everyone who trusts in Him.

sayings.text: O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!
sayings.speaker: Habakkuk, praying
sayings.why: Habakkuk saw violence all around him and felt unheard. Joseph Smith asked something like it in Liberty Jail: “How long shall thy hand be stayed” (D&C 121:2).

sayings.text: For, lo, I raise up the Chaldeans, that bitter and hasty nation
sayings.speaker: The Lord, to Habakkuk
sayings.why: This was the Lord’s answer to Habakkuk’s prayer: Babylon would come to punish Judah. The answer troubled Habakkuk even more (verses 12–13).

sayings.text: Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
sayings.speaker: Habakkuk, in his song
sayings.why: Habakkuk begins his book with hard questions and ends it singing. Even if every crop failed, he would still rejoice in the Lord (Habakkuk 3:17).

sayings.text: Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth
sayings.speaker: Zephaniah, to the humble
sayings.why: Before the day of judgment, Zephaniah invited the humble to seek the Lord, so they might be “hid in the day of the LORD’s anger.”

sayings.text: Sing, O daughter of Zion; shout, O Israel
sayings.speaker: Zephaniah, to Jerusalem
sayings.why: After all his warnings, Zephaniah ends with joy. The Lord will be in the midst of His people and rejoice over them (Zephaniah 3:17).

words.clue: they shall beat their ____ into plowshares
words.mean: In the last days, nations will turn their weapons into farm tools. When the Lord reigns, war will end.

words.clue: out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ____ in Israel
words.mean: Micah foretold that the Savior would be born in little Bethlehem, long before it happened.

words.clue: what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do ____
words.mean: The Lord asks us to be fair and honest, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with Him.

words.clue: thou wilt cast all their sins into the ____ of the sea
words.mean: When we repent, the Lord throws our sins far away, where they are gone for good.

words.clue: The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of ____
words.mean: When hard times come, the Lord is a safe place for everyone who trusts Him.

words.clue: the just shall live by his ____
words.mean: Righteous people keep trusting God and stay faithful to Him, even while they wait.

words.clue: he will joy over thee with ____
words.mean: The Lord is so glad to be with His faithful people that He rejoices over them.

deep.intro: The lesson asks what Micah 6:6–8 says matters most to the Lord. Before that answer, the chapter opens like a court case, with the Lord bringing charges against His people.
deep.q: In Micah 6:2, whom does the Lord call to hear His case against His people?
deep.why: Verse 2: “Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD’s controversy, and ye strong foundations of the earth.” A controversy here is a case in court, with the mountains as witnesses.
deep.find: Hear ye, O mountains, the LORD’s controversy
deep.hunt: In Micah 6, whom does the Lord call to hear His case against His people?

deep.intro: The lesson invites you to look in Nahum 1 for verses about the Lord’s power and His mercy. Read how Nahum pictures the power of the One who is also slow to anger.
deep.q: In Nahum 1:3, what does Nahum say the clouds are?
deep.why: Verse 3: “the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.” The clouds are like dust kicked up as He walks.
deep.find: the clouds are the dust of his feet
deep.hunt: In Nahum 1, what does Nahum say the clouds are?

deep.intro: The lesson asks what in Habakkuk 2:1–4 helps you trust the Lord when you have unanswered questions. Read what Habakkuk does while he waits for the Lord’s answer.
deep.q: In Habakkuk 2:1, where does Habakkuk go to wait for the Lord’s answer?
deep.right: Up on the tower, to watch
wrong: Out to the desert, to fast
deep.why: Verse 1: “I will stand upon my watch, and set me upon the tower, and will watch to see what he will say unto me.” He waited like a guard, ready for the answer.
deep.hunt: In Habakkuk 2, where does Habakkuk go to wait for the Lord’s answer?

deep.intro: The lesson invites you to look for the kind of people God would preserve. Near the end of his book, Zephaniah describes them.
deep.q: In Zephaniah 3:12, what will the afflicted and poor people the Lord leaves do?
deep.right: Trust in the name of the Lord
wrong: Rebuild the walls of the city
Go back to their own land
deep.why: Verse 12: “they shall trust in the name of the LORD.” Verse 13 adds that they won’t lie or do wrong. The humble and honest trust Him.
deep.find: they shall trust in the name of the LORD
deep.hunt: In Zephaniah 3, what will the afflicted and poor people the Lord leaves do?

deep.intro: The lesson suggests comparing Zephaniah 3:14–20 with 3 Nephi 17. Read how the risen Savior showed His joy in His people, and especially in their children.
deep.q: In 3 Nephi 17:21, what did Jesus do for the little children?
deep.right: Blessed them one by one, and prayed
wrong: Gave them bread and fish to eat
Taught them a song to sing
deep.why: Verse 21: “he took their little children, one by one, and blessed them, and prayed unto the Father for them.” Just before, He said His joy was full.
deep.find: he took their little children, one by one, and blessed them
deep.hunt: In 3 Nephi 17, what did Jesus do for the little children?

deep.title: From the children’s part of the lesson
deep.intro: The children’s part of this week’s lesson includes “Wait for it; because it will surely come” (Habakkuk 2:3). It suggests talking about good things that only come after we wait.
deep.q: The lesson gives two examples of good things you have to wait for. What are they?
deep.right: Fruit to ripen and dough to bake
wrong: Seeds to sprout and eggs to hatch
Snow to melt and flowers to bloom
deep.why: It mentions fruit that has to ripen and dough that has to bake. Eaten too soon, they aren’t ready yet. God’s promises come when they are ready.
deep.find: fruit that needs to ripen or dough that needs to bake

deep.title: From For the Strength of Youth
deep.intro: In this month’s For the Strength of Youth, Elder Quentin L. Cook writes that Jesus Christ gives us every reason to rejoice. Zephaniah told God’s people to sing and rejoice too.
deep.q: What does Elder Cook suggest inviting someone to this Christmas season?
deep.why: He says inviting someone to a Christmas sacrament meeting can help them feel the Spirit and remember Jesus Christ. Don’t worry about the outcome; the Savior magnifies sincere efforts.
deep.find: inviting someone to attend a Christmas sacrament meeting

reels.hook: Three things the Lord asks of you
reels.body: Micah sums up what the Lord wants in three things. Do justly: be fair and honest with God and with people. Love mercy: be kind and forgiving, the way He is with you. Walk humbly with God: stay close to Him and let Him lead. Jesus taught the same thing when He named the two great commandments: love God, and love your neighbor (Matthew 22:37–39).

verse.text: He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God?

question.q: What does the Lord ask of us in Micah 6:8?
question.right: Be just, love mercy, walk humbly with Him
wrong: Bring Him bigger and better offerings
Build Him a grander, richer temple
question.why: He asks us “to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God.” Not bigger offerings, but a changed heart and life.

bonus.q: This week’s Scripture Helps quote Elder Dale G. Renlund on Micah’s call to do justly. What does he say it means?
bonus.right: Act honorably with God and with others
wrong: Punish every person who does wrong
bonus.why: He says doing justly means acting honorably with God and with other people. We do that with God by walking humbly with Him, and with others by loving mercy.
bonus.find: To do justly means acting honorably with God and with other people

reels.hook: What gift could ever pay for sin?
reels.seek: Someone wonders if huge piles of offerings would make God happy
reels.body: Micah pictures someone asking how to make things right with God. Bring thousands of rams? Ten thousand rivers of olive oil? Even their own firstborn child? The answer is no. No offering, however huge, can pay for sin. Only Jesus Christ could do that. What the Lord asks of us is our hearts: to do justly, love mercy and walk humbly with Him (verse 8).

verse.text: Will the LORD be pleased with thousands of rams, or with ten thousands of rivers of oil? shall I give my firstborn for my transgression, the fruit of my body for the sin of my soul?

question.q: Why couldn’t thousands of rams make up for sin?
question.right: Only Jesus Christ can pay for sin
wrong: Rams cost too little to count
God wanted gold instead of rams
question.why: No offering was big enough, not even “thousands of rams.” Jesus Christ paid for sin. The Lord asks for our hearts.

bonus.q: In Micah 6:4, which three leaders does the Lord remind Israel that He sent before them?
bonus.hunt: In Micah 6, which three leaders does the Lord remind Israel that He sent before them?
bonus.why: Verse 4: “I brought thee up out of the land of Egypt… and I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam.” The Lord had always taken care of them.
bonus.find: I sent before thee Moses, Aaron, and Miriam

reels.hook: A safe fortress when hard times come
reels.body: Most of Nahum is about the fall of Nineveh, the capital of cruel Assyria, which had hurt God’s people for years. But in chapter 1 Nahum stops to say this. A strong hold is a fortress: thick walls on high ground, a safe place when enemies come. When hard times come, the Lord is that safe place, and He knows every person who trusts Him.

verse.text: The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.

question.q: What is the Lord like for the people who trust Him?
question.right: A fortress that keeps them safe
wrong: A judge who waits to punish them
A king who lives far away
question.why: “The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble.” A strong hold is a fortress, and He knows each one who trusts Him.

bonus.q: In Nahum 1:15, once the wicked enemy is cut off, what does Nahum tell Judah to keep?
bonus.hunt: In Nahum 1, once the wicked enemy is cut off, what does Nahum tell Judah to keep?
bonus.why: Verse 15: “O Judah, keep thy solemn feasts, perform thy vows: for the wicked shall no more pass through thee.” With Assyria gone, they could worship in peace.

reels.hook: He throws your sins where no one can reach them
reels.body: Micah’s own name asks a question: who is like the Lord? He ends his book asking it: “Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity” (Micah 7:18). The Lord doesn’t stay angry, “because he delighteth in mercy” (Micah 7:18). When we repent, He doesn’t keep our sins close by. He throws them into the deepest sea, where no one can bring them back.

verse.text: He will turn again, he will have compassion upon us; he will subdue our iniquities; and thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.

question.q: What does Micah say the Lord does with the sins of those who repent?
question.right: Throws them into the deep sea
wrong: Keeps them in a book forever
Hides them away in a box
question.why: “Thou wilt cast all their sins into the depths of the sea.” He doesn’t keep them nearby. He gets rid of them.

bonus.q: In Micah 7:8, what does Micah say the Lord will be to him when he sits in darkness?
bonus.hunt: In Micah 7, what does Micah say the Lord will be to him when he sits in darkness?
bonus.why: Verse 8: “when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.” Falling isn’t the end of the story.
bonus.find: the LORD shall be a light unto me

reels.hook: Even a prophet felt God wasn’t listening
reels.body: Habakkuk saw violence and fighting all around him, and his prayers didn’t seem to change anything. So he told the Lord exactly how he felt. Joseph Smith asked something like it in Liberty Jail: “O God, where art thou?” (D&C 121:1). It’s all right to bring hard questions to God. Habakkuk didn’t stop praying. He kept asking, and he kept listening for the answer.

verse.text: O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear! even cry out unto thee of violence, and thou wilt not save!

question.q: What did Habakkuk do when his prayers seemed unanswered?
question.right: Told God his worries and kept asking
wrong: Stopped praying and gave up on God
question.why: “O LORD, how long shall I cry, and thou wilt not hear!” He took his honest question straight to the Lord.

bonus.q: In Habakkuk 1:8, which animals does the Lord say the Chaldeans’ horses are swifter than?
bonus.hunt: In Habakkuk 1, which animals does the Lord say the Chaldeans’ horses are swifter than?
bonus.why: Verse 8: “Their horses also are swifter than the leopards, and are more fierce than the evening wolves.” Babylon’s army would come fast.

reels.hook: Still waiting? His promise is on its way.
reels.body: After Habakkuk’s questions, the Lord gave him a vision and told him it would come true at the time God had set. Even if it seemed slow: “wait for it; because it will surely come.” The lesson says spiritual answers take time too, and can’t be forced. God’s timing can feel late to us, but His promises always come.

verse.text: For the vision is yet for an appointed time, but at the end it shall speak, and not lie: though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come, it will not tarry.

question.q: What does the Lord tell Habakkuk to do about His promise?
question.right: Wait for it, because it will come
wrong: Give up if it doesn’t come soon
question.why: “Though it tarry, wait for it; because it will surely come.” Tarry means take a long time. His promises always come true.

bonus.q: In Habakkuk 2:2, what does the Lord tell Habakkuk to do with the vision?
bonus.hunt: In Habakkuk 2, what does the Lord tell Habakkuk to do with the vision?
wrong: Tell it only to the king
bonus.why: Verse 2: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it.” Tables here means tablets.
bonus.find: Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables

reels.hook: Crops gone, flocks gone, and still full of joy
reels.body: Habakkuk started his book upset and asking hard questions. He ends it singing. In verse 17 he pictures losing everything a farmer needs: figs, grapes, olives, crops, sheep and cattle. Then he says, “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD.” His joy didn’t depend on how things turned out. It came from the God he trusted.

verse.text: Although the fig tree shall not blossom, neither shall fruit be in the vines; … Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.

question.q: Why could Habakkuk rejoice even if his crops failed?
question.right: His joy came from the Lord, not his farm
wrong: He knew the rain would come next week
He had plenty of food saved up
question.why: “Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.” Things could go wrong. The Lord would not.

bonus.q: In Habakkuk 3:11, what does Habakkuk say stood still?
bonus.hunt: In Habakkuk 3, what does Habakkuk say stood still?
bonus.why: Verse 11: “The sun and moon stood still in their habitation.” He remembers Joshua’s day, when the Lord fought for Israel (Joshua 10:12–14).
bonus.find: The sun and moon stood still in their habitation

reels.hook: A tiny town, picked centuries ahead
reels.body: About 700 years before Jesus was born, Micah named the little town He would come from: Bethlehem. When Wise Men came to Jerusalem asking where the new King was born, Herod’s advisers found the answer in Micah’s words (Matthew 2:5–6). God made that promise long before, and He kept it right on time. He keeps His promises to you too.

verse.text: But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah, though thou be little among the thousands of Judah, yet out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel; whose goings forth have been from of old, from everlasting.

question.q: How did Herod’s advisers know where Jesus would be born?
question.right: Micah had prophesied it long before
wrong: The Wise Men had a map to it
An angel told King Herod in a dream
question.why: Micah wrote, “But thou, Beth-lehem Ephratah… out of thee shall he come forth unto me that is to be ruler in Israel.” His word came true.

bonus.q: In Micah 5:4, what will this ruler do in the strength of the Lord?
bonus.hunt: In Micah 5, what will this ruler do in the strength of the Lord?
wrong: Sit on a throne of gold
bonus.why: Verse 4: “he shall stand and feed in the strength of the LORD.” Feeding is what a shepherd does for his flock.

reels.hook: Humble hearts find a hiding place
reels.body: Zephaniah warned that a day of judgment was coming on the proud. But first he gave an invitation: seek the Lord, seek righteousness, seek meekness. Meek doesn’t mean weak. It means humble and willing to be taught. The promise for the meek: “it may be ye shall be hid in the day of the LORD’s anger.” Jesus taught it too: “Blessed are the meek” (Matthew 5:5).

verse.text: Seek ye the LORD, all ye meek of the earth, which have wrought his judgment; seek righteousness, seek meekness: it may be ye shall be hid in the day of the LORD’s anger.

question.q: What three things does Zephaniah tell the meek to seek?
wrong: Riches, honor, and a long life
question.why: “Seek ye the LORD… seek righteousness, seek meekness.” The humble can be sheltered when hard times come.

bonus.hunt: In Zephaniah 2, what did proud Nineveh say in her heart?
bonus.right: I am, and there is none beside me
wrong: I will repent and serve the Lord
My walls will fall one day soon
bonus.why: Verse 15: she “said in her heart, I am, and there is none beside me.” That’s pride: thinking you need no one, not even God.

reels.hook: God searches every corner with a lamp
reels.body: Zephaniah described people who thought God didn’t care what they did. They said, “The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil.” The Lord said He would search Jerusalem with candles, like someone hunting through a dark house for something lost. The Old Testament Student Manual explains that “settled on their lees” compares lazy hearts to wine left sitting too long, getting thick and bitter.

verse.text: And it shall come to pass at that time, that I will search Jerusalem with candles, and punish the men that are settled on their lees: that say in their heart, The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil.

question.q: What did the people in Zephaniah 1:12 think about God?
question.right: That He wouldn’t do anything at all
wrong: That He would come to save them soon
That He was angry with everyone
question.why: They said, “The LORD will not do good, neither will he do evil.” They thought He didn’t notice. He notices everything.

bonus.hunt: In Zephaniah 1, where were people worshipping the host of heaven?
bonus.why: Verse 5: “them that worship the host of heaven upon the housetops.” The host of heaven means false gods tied to the stars and planets.

reels.hook: The Lord sings over you with joy
reels.body: After all of Zephaniah’s warnings, his book ends with a song. The Lord, the King of Israel, will be right in the midst of His people. He “will rejoice over thee with joy.” He “will joy over thee with singing.” The lesson invites us to compare this with 3 Nephi 17, when the risen Jesus stood among the Nephites and said His joy was full. That’s how He feels about His people, including you.

verse.text: The LORD thy God in the midst of thee is mighty; he will save, he will rejoice over thee with joy; he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing.

question.q: How does Zephaniah 3:17 say the Lord feels about His faithful people?
question.right: He is so glad He sings over them
wrong: He puts up with them, but barely
He is too busy to notice them
question.why: “He will rejoice over thee with joy… he will joy over thee with singing.” The Lord is happy to be with His people.

bonus.q: In Zephaniah 3:16, what will be said to Jerusalem in that day?
bonus.hunt: In Zephaniah 3, what will be said to Jerusalem in that day?
bonus.why: Verse 16: “In that day it shall be said to Jerusalem, Fear thou not.” With the Lord in their midst, there’s nothing to fear.
bonus.find: it shall be said to Jerusalem, Fear thou not

reels.hook: The whole world comes to learn at His house
reels.body: Micah saw the last days. The Lord’s house would stand like the highest mountain, and people from many nations would stream to it to learn His ways. Then they would beat their swords into plowshares, tools for farming, and stop learning war (verse 3). Isaiah saw the same thing (Isaiah 2:2–4). Today temples are rising all over the earth, and people still go there to learn of Him.

verse.text: And many nations shall come, and say, Come, and let us go up to the mountain of the LORD, and to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths: for the law shall go forth of Zion, and the word of the LORD from Jerusalem.

question.q: In Micah 4:2, why do the nations go up to the Lord’s house?
question.right: So He can teach them His ways
wrong: To bring Him their taxes and tribute
To hide from an enemy army
question.why: “He will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” His house is a place to learn from Him.

bonus.q: In Micah 4:4, where will every man sit, with no one to make him afraid?
bonus.hunt: In Micah 4, where will every man sit, with no one to make him afraid?
bonus.right: Under his vine and fig tree
bonus.why: Verse 4: “they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid.” It’s a picture of peace at home.

lines: Micah, a prophet in the days of three kings of Judah, receives the word of the Lord about Samaria and Jerusalem. (verse 1)
The Lord is coming to judge. Samaria, the capital of Israel, will become a heap of stones, and its idols will be broken. (verses 2–7)
Micah mourns, because the same sickness has spread to Judah and reached the gate of Jerusalem. (verses 8–9)
He names town after town in Judah that will weep, and their children will be taken captive. (verses 10–16)
Woe to people who lie awake planning evil, then take other families’ fields and houses by force. (verses 1–2)
So the Lord will bring trouble on them, and their land will be divided up among others. (verses 3–5)
The people tell true prophets to stop, but they would gladly follow a prophet who promised them wine. (verses 6–11)
Still, the Lord will gather the remnant of Israel like sheep in a fold and lead them out as their King. (verses 12–13)
Micah tells Israel’s leaders they hate good and love evil and devour God’s people. When they cry to the Lord, He won’t answer. (verses 1–4)
False prophets promise peace to anyone who feeds them, but Micah is full of power by the Spirit of the Lord. (verses 5–8)
Judges take bribes, priests teach for pay, and prophets prophesy for money. So Jerusalem will be plowed like a field. (verses 9–12)

review.about: The heading’s “divine for money” is put as “prophesy for money,” as the plain words and the BSB read it.

lines: In the last days the house of the Lord will rise above the mountains, and people from many nations will go there to learn His ways. (verses 1–2)
Nations will beat their swords into farm tools and stop learning war, in the time of peace the Lord brings in the Millennium. (verses 3–5)
The Lord will gather His scattered and hurting people and reign over them in Zion forever. (verses 6–8)
First Jerusalem will suffer and go to Babylon, but the Lord will redeem her there and make her strong against her enemies. (verses 9–13)

review.about: “The Millennium” comes from the chapter heading (“the millennial era will commence”); the verses describe the peace without naming it.

lines: Out of little Bethlehem will come a ruler whose goings forth are from everlasting: the Messiah, Jesus Christ. (verses 1–2)
He will be great to the ends of the earth. He will be their peace and save them from Assyria. (verses 3–6)
In the last days the remnant of Jacob will be like dew from the Lord, and will triumph over the Gentiles like a lion. (verses 7–9)
The Lord will take away their chariots, witchcraft and idols, and judge the nations that would not obey. (verses 10–15)

review.about: The heading and Scripture Helps name the ruler as the Messiah; Matthew 2:5–6 applies it to Jesus.

insights.title: Joseph’s Bible: four books marked correct
insights.text: Joseph Smith worked through the whole Old Testament for his inspired revision of the Bible. His scribe, Frederick G. Williams, wrote down each change in a manuscript. Next to Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk and Zephaniah he wrote one word: “Correct.” The manuscript lists no changes for any of these four books.

insights.title: Puns in a sad song
insights.text: In Micah 1:10–16, Micah mourns over towns in Judah, and he plays on their names. George A. Pierce explains that one town’s name means “House of Dust,” so Micah tells it to roll in the dust. And “Declare ye it not at Gath” echoes David’s lament for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:20). Micah’s sad song was carefully made.

source.title: Understanding Micah’s Lament for Judah (Micah 1:10–16) through Text, Archaeology, and Geography

insights.title: Plotting in bed
insights.text: Micah 2:1 describes people who “devise iniquity, and work evil upon their beds.” The Old Testament Student Manual explains that they probably lay awake at night thinking up evil things to do, then did them as soon as it was light. Their plans? Taking fields and houses from families who couldn’t fight back.

insights.find: probably referring to those who lay awake at night thinking up evil things to do

insights.title: Prophets for hire, and a true one
insights.text: In Micah’s day some prophets said whatever paid. Dr. Joshua Sears explains that they promised peace to anyone who fed them. Micah was different: “full of power by the spirit of the LORD,” he told the people about their sins. Dr. Sears calls that the burden of true prophets. “They have to tell the people what they don’t want to hear.”

source.title: Old Testament: EPISODE 48 – Jonah, Micah – Part 2

insights.find: And that’s the burden of the true prophets. They have to tell the people what they don’t want to hear.

paras: Micah lived among prophets who would say whatever paid. In Micah 3:5 they “bite with their teeth, and cry, Peace.” Dr. Joshua Sears reads it this way: they promised peace to people who gave them something to eat and turned against anyone who didn’t. By verse 11 the judges, priests and prophets are all working for money, and still they say the Lord is among them.

Micah set himself against them: “But truly I am full of power by the spirit of the LORD.” Dr. Sears calls this the burden of the true prophets. “They have to tell the people what they don’t want to hear.” Hank Smith adds that no one was paying Micah to say it.

Dr. Sears compares Micah with President Russell M. Nelson, who at a BYU devotional described the burden the prophetic mantle places on him: “The arbiter of truth is God not your favorite social media newsfeed.” Apostles are commanded to teach truth, even when they are called uncaring for it. Micah felt that same weight, Dr. Sears says, because he truly had the Spirit, and with it the duty to declare transgression and sin.

insights.title: Streaming up to the temples
insights.text: Micah saw that in the last days people would “flow unto” the mountain of the Lord’s house. Noe Correa, writing for Scripture Central, sees it happening now. In the Restoration, the Lord’s people go up to His temples to make covenants with Him. And at almost every general conference, the prophet announces more temples around the world.

insights.find: In the restoration, the Lord’s modern Israel has flowed up to the mountain-temples to receive and make covenants with Him

insights.title: Babylon, named early
insights.text: Micah told Jerusalem, “thou shalt go even to Babylon; there shalt thou be delivered.” The Old Testament Student Manual points out why that is amazing. In Micah’s day Assyria ruled the world, and Babylon was only one of its provinces. Micah was seeing nearly 130 years ahead, to the captivity and to the Lord redeeming His people from it.

source.title: Promise of Judgments, Promise of Salvation (Micah)

insights.find: This prophecy is amazing because Assyria was mistress of the world in Micah’s day, Babylon being only a province of Assyria

insights.title: Jesus quoted Micah
insights.text: On His second day with the Nephites, the risen Jesus quoted Micah and Isaiah so much that exactly half the verses of His sermon came from them. He used Micah 5:8–9 and 4:12–13 (3 Nephi 20:15–20). Scripture Central explains that His theme was the Father’s covenant with Israel, a covenant He has never forgotten.

source.title: Why Did Jesus Mix Together Micah and Isaiah?

insights.find: exactly half of the verses in the speech come from these prophets

insights.title: Which Bethlehem?
insights.text: Why does Micah say “Beth-lehem Ephratah” and not just Bethlehem? The Old Testament Student Manual explains that there was another Bethlehem, in the land given to the tribe of Zebulun (Joshua 19:15). Ephratah marks the Bethlehem in Judah, the town where Jesus was born (Matthew 2:1).

source.title: Promise of Judgments, Promise of Salvation (Micah)

insights.find: Ephratah is simply an additional name to distinguish the Bethlehem in Judah from another Bethlehem in the land assigned to the tribe of Zebulun

insights.quote: How appropriate it was that He, the “bread of life,” was to come from the “house of bread.”
insights.text: Micah 5:2 names Bethlehem as the Savior’s birthplace. Elder Nelson notes that Bethlehem means house of bread in Hebrew, and Jesus called Himself the bread of life (John 6:48).

insights.title: Like dew on the grass
insights.text: Micah says the remnant of Jacob will be “as a dew from the LORD, as the showers upon the grass.” Blair G. Van Dyke and D. Kelly Ogden explain that people who keep their lives focused on the Savior will be like nourishing dew and life-saving rain to the rest of the world.

insights.title: Caring, not judging
insights.text: Elder Dale G. Renlund remembers a tired young doctor who complained about caring for a patient whose illness was his own fault. Her supervisor answered quietly: “You didn’t become a physician to judge them.” Elder Renlund says loving mercy means we aren’t judgmental. We’re glad when God shows others the same mercy He shows us.

source.title: Do Justly, Love Mercy, and Walk Humbly with God

insights.find: Loving mercy means that we do not just love the mercy God extends to us; we delight that God extends the same mercy to others

insights.quote: Without the blessings that come from Heavenly Father and Jesus Christ, we can never do enough or be enough by ourselves.
insights.text: Verses 6–7 ask whether huge offerings could pay for sin. Elder Renlund answers no, and then shares the good news: through Jesus Christ we can become enough.

insights.title: The love God shows, and asks for
insights.text: The Hebrew word behind “mercy” in Micah 6:8 is hesed: God’s loving-kindness, faithfulness and steadfast love. David Rolph Seely points out that the kindness God shows His children is also something He asks His covenant people to show. God invites us to become like Him by doing what He does.

source.title: Tender Mercies and Loving-Kindness

insights.find: Such actions are also an obligation placed on the Lord’s covenant people

insights.title: A name that asks a question
insights.text: Micah’s name, like Michael, means “like unto Jehovah.” His book ends by asking, “Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity”? Noe Correa, writing for Scripture Central, says the prophet’s name and this closing question are bookends around the whole book.

source.title: Old Testament Minute: Micah

insights.find: The name of the prophet and this closing statement serve as bookends

insights.title: He loves to forgive
insights.text: Micah says the Lord “delighteth in mercy.” Dr. Joshua Sears explains that mercy here is the Hebrew hesed, God’s covenant love and loyalty. God isn’t grumbling when He forgives. He loves it. And in verse 19 the word for “cast” is like hurling. He doesn’t hide our sins in a closet. He throws them into the depths of the sea.

source.title: Old Testament: EPISODE 48 – Jonah, Micah – Part 2

insights.find: He delights in extending that love and mercy and loyalty to us. It’s not like he’s grumbling about it.

paras: Dr. Joshua Sears points out that Micah’s name means “who is like,” and the book ends playing on it. In Micah 7:18 the prophet asks God, “Who is a God like unto thee, that pardoneth iniquity”? He “retaineth not his anger for ever, because he delighteth in mercy.”

The Hebrew word for mercy there is hesed, the covenant love President Russell M. Nelson wrote about in the October 2022 Liahona: a love and loyalty between God and those who make covenants with Him. Dr. Sears stresses that God is not grudging about it. “He loves extending mercy. He loves forgiving.”

Verse 19 says He will “cast all their sins into the depths of the sea,” and Dr. Sears says the verb is like hurling something. The Lord doesn’t sweep sins under a rug or shut them in a closet. He takes them to the edge of the cliff and throws them as far as He can. Verse 20 uses hesed again, “the mercy to Abraham,” the covenant God swore to keep, no matter how long it takes.

Dr. Sears ends with a promise for anyone who wonders if they, or someone they love, have gone too far. No one is so far gone that the light of that covenant love can’t reach them. As soon as we turn to Him and sincerely repent, “he will delight in forgetting all that happened.”

insights.title: Nahum means comforter
insights.text: Nahum’s name comes from a Hebrew root meaning to comfort, so it means comforter. Terry B. Ball compares Nahum’s message to watching a replay of a game you already know your team won. The close plays don’t worry you much. Nahum promised God’s people that their cruel enemy would fall. In the end, God triumphs over the adversary.

insights.find: Nahum is typically understood to mean a comforter or consoler

insights.title: Justice and mercy, both
insights.text: Nahum says the Lord “is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked,” and also that He “is good.” Ellis T. Rasmussen, quoted in the Old Testament Student Manual, sums it up: His mercy won’t rob justice, and His justice won’t rob His mercy. He is both powerful and merciful.

source.title: ‘The Burden of Ninevah’ (Nahum)

insights.title: Run to Him for shelter
insights.text: “The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.” Dr. Joshua Matson explains that the Hebrew behind “trust in him” better reads “those who seek refuge in Him.” It isn’t only believing God can help. It’s choosing to run to Him for shelter.

source.title: Old Testament: EPISODE 49 – Nahum; Habakkuk; Zephaniah – Part 1

insights.find: it’s this intentionality of finding refuge in God

paras: Dr. Joshua Matson suggests reading Nahum by first asking the disciples’ question, “Lord, is it I?” Chapter 1 pictures Jehovah as a warrior fighting the battles of His covenant people, so mighty that the mountains quake and the hills melt before Him.

Then comes verse 7, which John Bytheway calls the positive verse in the middle of it all: “The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble.” Dr. Matson notes that the Hebrew behind “them that trust in him” better reads “those who seek refuge in Him.” It isn’t only knowing that God can do these things. It is the deliberate choice to find refuge in Him.

That choice, he says, is what separates the covenant people from those who are destroyed later in the book. At the end of Nahum, Assyria’s shepherds slumber and its people are scattered, with no one to gather them (Nahum 3:18). Nineveh trusted the wrong shepherd. “But we are disciples of the Good Shepherd,” Dr. Matson says, and if we find refuge in Him, we will be protected.

insights.text: Nahum 1:7 promises that the Lord knows those who trust Him. Elder Gong teaches what that trust can do with our hardest days.

insights.title: The river gates open
insights.text: Nahum saw that “the gates of the rivers shall be opened, and the palace shall be dissolved.” Wally Breitenstein, writing for Scripture Central, explains that these were probably sluice gates, which control the flow of water. Archaeologists have learned that the Khosr River, which ran through the middle of Nineveh, overran the city.

source.title: Old Testament Minute: Nahum

insights.find: Nineveh was overrun by the Khosr River, which was a tributary of the Tigris River and ran through the center of Nineveh

insights.title: No better than Thebes
insights.text: Nahum asks Nineveh, “Art thou better than populous No”? No was Thebes, a great city in Egypt that Assyria itself had captured in 663 BC. Sidney B. Sperry explains that this helps date Nahum: after Thebes fell, but before Nineveh fell in 612 BC. Nineveh was no better than Thebes, and it would fall too.

source.title: ‘The Burden of Ninevah’ (Nahum)

insights.title: Wrestling with God in prayer
insights.text: Dr. Joshua Matson says Habakkuk’s name is close to a Hebrew word for clasp or embrace, and he pictures a wrestler’s hold. In chapters 1 and 2 Habakkuk wrestles with God in prayer, asking hard questions and listening for answers. “Friends, I think God can handle it,” Dr. Matson tells his students.

source.title: Old Testament: EPISODE 49 – Nahum; Habakkuk; Zephaniah – Part 2

insights.find: Habakkuk is amazingly fit for this idea of a wrestle

paras: Dr. Joshua Matson notes that the root of Habakkuk’s name is uncertain, but it is close to a word used in Genesis for unfolding, clasping or embracing. He hears two pictures in it: the embrace of family, and the hold of a wrestler, like Jacob wrestling the angel (Genesis 32:24). The second fits best, he says, because chapters 1 and 2 go back and forth between Habakkuk’s prayers and Jehovah’s answers.

Habakkuk’s first prayer, in verses 2–4, asks why God isn’t listening and why He lets injustice go on. Dr. Matson hears the same cry in Psalm 13 and in Joseph Smith’s plea from Liberty Jail (D&C 121:1–3). Many people tell him they feel their prayers hit the ceiling and fall back to the floor. “And that’s Habakkuk,” he says.

His counsel is not to be afraid of that wrestle: “Friends, I think God can handle it.” John Bytheway adds that the cry of “how long” isn’t unbelief. It is faith asking how long it has to wait. Habakkuk keeps praying, and the Lord answers him.

insights.text: Nephi wrote that in Lehi’s day “many prophets” warned Jerusalem to repent (1 Nephi 1:4). Scripture Central counts nine Bible prophets active in those years, a remarkably high number. Zephaniah is on the list, along with Nahum, Habakkuk and Jeremiah. Lehi was not the only voice warning Jerusalem.

insights.title: A name that means hidden
insights.text: Zephaniah’s name comes from a Hebrew root meaning to hide, protect or treasure up. It can mean one who is hidden or protected by the Lord. Terry B. Ball points to the wordplay in Zephaniah 2:3, where the meek may be “hid in the day of the LORD’s anger.” In righteous King Josiah’s day, Jerusalem was spared.

insights.title: A tale of two cities
insights.text: Dr. Joshua Matson reads Zephaniah 3 as two cities. Verses 1–13 describe a proud, oppressing city under a “woe.” Verses 14–20 are a song for Jerusalem, the city of peace, where “the LORD, is in the midst of thee.” Which city do we want to live in? Zephaniah sets them side by side and lets us choose.

source.title: Old Testament: EPISODE 49 – Nahum; Habakkuk; Zephaniah – Part 2

insights.find: Which city do we want to take up residency in?

paras: Dr. Joshua Matson notes that Zephaniah, unlike Nahum and Habakkuk, dates himself exactly: the days of King Josiah (Zephaniah 1:1). The book could almost be read as one long chapter, he says, but it has key moments: doom announced, one last chance to repent in chapter 2, and then a proud city set against a city of peace.

Zephaniah 3:1–13 is a woe on “the oppressing city,” which “obeyed not the voice.” Some call it the woe against the oppressive city, Dr. Matson says, because the text never says which city it is. Any city that oppresses can hear what God will do, and any reader can ask whether he lives there.

Then verses 14–20 burst into a song for Jerusalem. Dr. Matson hears the earlier books answered. Habakkuk had asked, “Why dost thou shew me iniquity” (Habakkuk 1:3), and now the Lord promises, “thou shalt not see evil any more.” After a week of woes, he asks, what better way to end than with God in the midst of His people?
